Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 101, verse 1–3:

Surah al-Qari'ah

Meccan, without any disagreement, and its verses number eleven according to the Kufan reckoning, ten according to the Hijazi, and eight according to the Basran and Syrian. Its connection to what precedes it is too evident to need mention.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿The Striking Calamity﴾ ﴿What is the Striking Calamity?﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what the Striking Calamity is?﴾ The majority hold that it is the Resurrection itself, its beginning being the first blast of the Trumpet (nafkhah) and its end being the final judgment (fasl al-qada') among the creatures. It has also been said that it is the sound of the blast. Al-Dahhak said: it is the Fire, which has fury and roaring, but this is not correct. In any case, it derives from al-qar' (qar'), which is striking with force, such that a loud sound results from it. The discussion of it has already passed, and likewise what is known of its grammatical analysis (i'rab) of what was mentioned in the discussion of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿The Inevitable Reality﴾ ﴿What is the Inevitable Reality?﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what the Inevitable Reality is?﴾. ʿIsa read: «al-qari'ata» in the accusative, and it is interpreted as being governed by an implied verb, i.e., "mention the Striking Calamity."

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 101, verse 4:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿On the Day when mankind will be like scattered moths﴾. It was also said: it is in the accusative case (*manṣūb*) by an implied verb, *udhkur* ("remember"; the imperative, Arabic اذْكُرْ), as if it were said, after magnifying the matter of the Striking Calamity (*al-qāri'ah*) and making the Messenger (upon him be blessings and peace) eager to know it: "Remember the Day when mankind will be..." etc. ﴿And what will make you know what the Striking Calamity is?﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an adverbial of time (*ẓarf*) governed by an implied verb indicated by *al-qāri'ah*; that is, "it strikes on the Day." Al-Hufi said: it is an adverbial of time that comes as a dependent element (*ẓarf ta'attā muqaddaran*). Some have supposed this verb to be placed before *al-qāri'ah*, making it the subject of that verb too. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is an adverbial of time for *al-qāri'ah* itself, without any implied verb, but he did not specify which of the calamities he meant. Abu Hayyan objected to him: if he meant the first word, then the objection is that it separates the governing word, which is within the relative clause (*ṣilah*) of *al*, from the governed element, which is the predicate (*khabar*), and this is not permitted; and if he meant the second or third, then the meaning of the adverbial of time does not fit with it. It is supported by the reading of Zayd ibn 'Ali, *yawmu* ("Day") in the nominative (*raf'*), on this basis; and some have supposed the subject to be "its time" (*waqtuhā*).

As for *al-farāsh* (moths): in *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* it says: it is the plural of *farāshah*, the one that flies and hurls itself into the fire; and this is what is narrated from Qatadah. It was also said: it is a delicate bird that makes for the fire and never stops charging at the lamp or the like until it burns.

Al-Farra' said: it is the swarm of locusts that spreads over the earth and piles up on one another out of terror. The author of *al-Ta'wilat* said: they have differed in its interpretation in several ways; but all of them return to one meaning, namely an indication of bewilderment and agitation because of the terror of that Day. Many have chosen what is narrated from Qatadah, and they said: they are likened in their multitude, their dispersal, their weakness, their humiliation, their coming and going without order, and their flying toward the caller from every direction when he calls them to the place of gathering, to scattered, flying moths. Jarir said:

*Indeed, al-Farazdaq, as far as I know, and his people,*
*are like moths that flock to the fire of one who warms himself.*

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 101, verse 5:

﴿And the mountains will be like wool(ʿihn)﴾ — i.e., wool in general, or dyed wool, as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) restricted it. The discussion of this word has already passed in (surah) al-Ma'arij. Here the verb "kana" carries the meaning of "sara" (became), i.e., all the mountains will become like wool.

﴿scattered(al-manfush)﴾ — meaning separated by the finger or the like, in the dispersal of its parts and their scattering through the air, as other verses also indicate.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 101, verses 6–7:

The Almighty's saying, ﴿So as for him whose scales are heavy﴾ and to the end of the verse, is a general statement dividing people into two groups, and an indication of the particular states of each of them after the explanation of the states common to all.

This refers to the weighing of deeds. It is one of the matters that must be believed in as a reality, and whoever denies it is not declared a disbeliever. It takes place after the scrolls have been scattered and taken in the right hand and the left hand, and after the questioning and the reckoning, as al-Wahidi and others have mentioned. The author of Kanz al-Asrar (Treasury of Secrets) asserted it, saying that there is a scale with a tongue and two pans, like the enfolding of the heavens and the earth, and Allah the Most High knows best its reality. The view that this is so has been related from Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan al-Basri, and Sharh al-Maqasid (the commentary on al-Maqasid) attributes it to many commentators. Its location is between Paradise and Hell, as in Nawadir al-Usul (Rare Principles of Jurisprudence), which mentions: "The scale is held by the Throne. Jibril, peace be upon him, takes hold of its pillar, looking at its tongue, and Mika'il, peace be upon him, is its trustee." The most famous and most correct view is that it is one scale, as we have mentioned, for all nations and all deeds. Thus the Almighty's saying ﴿its scales﴾ is the plural of mizan (scale), and its original form is muwzan with a waw, but it was changed into a ya' because it is sukun (quiescent) and the letter before it is kasra (vowel-i). It is said that the plural is for magnification, like the plural in the Almighty's saying ﴿The people of 'Ad denied the messengers﴾, according to one view. Or it is in terms of its parts, as in the expression shabat mufariquhu ("his parting hair turned grey"). Or it is in terms of the multiplicity of individual instances, because of the conceptual variety, as has been said about the line:

"The gleam of lightning or the rays of suns."

Al-Razi, as is reported from him, claimed that there is a hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) on this point. Others said: the deeds themselves are weighed, so good deeds are imagined in beautiful luminous forms and then placed in the pan of light, which is the right pan prepared for good deeds, so it becomes heavy by the grace of Allah the Most High. Evil deeds are imagined in ugly dark forms and then placed in the pan of darkness, which is the left, so it becomes light by the justice of Allah the Most High. The impossibility of transforming realities in the sphere of breaking customary patterns is either prohibited or restricted to the persistence of the traces of the original reality. Some scholars held that Allah the Most High creates bodies equal in number to those deeds, without transforming them, and claimed that there is a report about this. The apparent meaning is that heaviness and lightness are like them in this world: what is heavy goes down, then rises to 'Illiyyun (the highest level), and what is light is carried up, then descends to Sijjin (the lowest register). Al-Qurtubi stated this explicitly. Some later scholars said: they are contrary to what is in this world, so that the deed of the believer, when it outweighs, ascends, and his evil deeds become heavy, and that the disbeliever's pan becomes heavy because the other pan is empty of good deeds. Then he recited: ﴿And the good deed raises it﴾. Whether this is evidence is open to question. Some mentioned that the description of the weighing is that all the deeds of the servants are placed in the scale at one time: the good deeds in the pan of light, on the right of the Throne toward Paradise, and the evil deeds in the pan of darkness toward Hell. Allah the Most High creates for every person a necessary knowledge by which he perceives the lightness and heaviness of his deeds. It was said similarly, except that the sign of preponderance is a pillar of light that rises from the pan of good deeds until it covers the pan of evil deeds, and the sign of lightness is a pillar of darkness that rises from the pan of evil deeds until it covers the pan of good deeds. So the states are four, and the true condition will become apparent by direct sight. As al-Qurtubi said, this does not apply to every individual, because of the authentic hadith: "It will be said: O Muhammad, admit into Paradise from your nation those who have no reckoning, through the right-hand gate," and so on in the hadith. The prophets, peace be upon them, are even more deserving of this. The Almighty's saying ﴿The criminals will be known by their marks, and they will be seized by the forelocks and the feet﴾ also (applies). The weighing remains only for whomever Allah the Most High wills from the two groups. Al-Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id al-Ballluti mentioned that the people of patience do not have their deeds weighed, but rather their reward is poured out for them in full.

[Page 222]

The apparent meaning is that the hypocrite is included among the disbelievers. The truth is that their deeds in general are weighed, according to the apparent meaning of the verses and the many hadiths. The meaning in the verse is a beneficial weighing. The correct view is that the jinn, believing and disbelieving, are like humankind in this matter, as has been established in its proper place. The division in what we are discussing, according to what you have heard from al-Qurtubi, applies to those whose deeds are weighed, not to people in general without qualification. The Mu'tazila denied that the weighing is real. A group of Ahl al-Sunna, including Mujahid, al-Dahhak and al-A'mash, said: deeds are accidents (a'rad); if their continuation is possible, their weighing is not possible. So the weighing is an expression for the upright judgment and the just ruling. In this verse they allowed that mawazin (scales) could be the plural of mawzun (the thing weighed), meaning the deed that has weight and worth before Allah the Most High, and that its heaviness means its preponderance. This was related from al-Farra'. That is, ﴿whoever's good deeds are weighty in their measures and ranks﴾. ﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾. The well-known view is to take this as the relative form (nisba): that is, possessing satisfaction. It was also permitted that "pleasing" (radiya) means "pleased with" (mardiyya) in a transferred sense in the word itself, and that the attribution be figurative, while the attribution to the possessor of the life is literal. It was also permitted that there be a metaphor, either implicit or imaginative, in the speech, as established in the books of rhetoric. However, one of the eminent scholars made a precious statement here: that what is in the relative form is interpreted as "possessing such-and-such," so it is not feminized, since it does not describe a noun and so it is attached to the non-derived nouns. It is related from al-Sirafi that he said: what they gave as reasoning is open to objection regarding the dropping of the ha' in ﴿a pleasing life﴾, and there are two views on it. One is that it means that the life is pleasing to its people, so it is constantly with them, and they are pleased with it. The other is that the ha' is for intensification, like allama (very knowing) and rawwaya (great narrator). It was explained that the ha' is obligatory so that the ya' does not drop out and damage the form, as in naqa mushliya (a she-camel that has given birth) and kalba mujriya (a bitch that has borne young). They say zabya mutfil and mushdin (a gazelle with a young one, a gazelle with a fawn that has grown), and the pattern mif'al and mif'al is not feminized. They have added the ha' to some of it, as in misakka. The end of his words.

Then he said: this is worthy of acceptance, and its essence is an answer in several ways. First: radiya here is not from the relative form, but is an active participle, by which is meant the necessary sense of its meaning, because whoever wills something and is pleased with it stays with it. So it is a metonymy or a metaphor. It is possible that what is meant is that it is a figurative attribution, and what was mentioned explains its second meaning. Second: the ha' is for intensification and is not restricted to fa'al, which is why he also gave the example rawwaya. Third: it is permitted to add the ha' to the weak-letter (mu'tall) forms to preserve the structure, and misakka is either irregular, or it is for the assimilation of the doubled form to the weak-letter form. End of quotation. So remember this, for it is precious, and most books are free of it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 101, verses 8–11:

﴿And as for he whose scales are light﴾ — meaning, one who has no good deed of any account, or whose evil deeds outweigh his good deeds. ﴿Then his mother﴾ — that is, his refuge (ma'wah), as said by Ibn Zayd and others. ﴿Is an abyss (hawiyah)﴾ — by which is meant the Fire, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And what will make you know what it is? A Fire, blazing hot.﴾

This is a confirmation of it after its vagueness, and an indication that it has departed from what is familiar, for the sake of magnification and awe. It has been mentioned that applying this name to it is due to the extreme depth of its pit and the distance of its fall. It has been narrated that the people of the Fire will fall into it for seventy autumns. Some have restricted it to the lowest gate of the Fire. He expressed the refuge by "mother" by way of likening it to a mother, for a mother is a child's place of refuge and shelter, and in this there is mockery of him. It has been said: He likened the Fire to a mother in that it encompasses him as the womb of a mother encompasses the child. And from Qatadah, Abu Salih, Ikrimah, al-Kalbi and others: the meaning is "his head's mother is an abyss at the bottom of Hell," because he will be cast into it upside down. In another narration from Qatadah, it is from their saying when they invoke ruin upon a man: "May his mother be bereft (hawat ummuhu)," because when he falls (hawa), that is, drops and perishes, then his mother has been bereaved, through loss and grief. From this is the saying of Ka'b ibn Sa'd al-Ghanawi:

"May his mother be bereft, what the dawn sends forth at morning, and what the night returns with when it comes back."

In al-Kashf it is said that this is better, to correspond with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿In a pleasing life﴾, and with what it contains of exaggeration. Al-Tibi said: it is the more apparent, and there is room for discussion regarding it. The pronoun, I mean "hiya" in it, refers to the calamity indicated by the speech, and to what we have mentioned for "hawiyah." And on the second interpretation, it refers to what the speech implies, as if it were said: "Then his head's mother is an abyss in a fire, and what will make you know what it is," etc.

The hā' attached in ﴿hiyah﴾ is the hā' of pausing (hā' al-sakt), and Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-A'mash and Hamzah omitted it in connected speech, while the majority kept it. ﴿Fire﴾ is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "it is a fire." "Blazing hot" (hamiyah) is its adjective, and it is from al-hummā, meaning the intensification of heat. In al-Qamus: "The sun and the fire were hot (hamā al-shamsu wa al-nāru) with hamyan, humiyyan and hamwan: their heat intensified." Some have taken it, as has been said, from "the cooking pot became heated (hamiyat al-qidr), so it is mahmiyyah," and so explained it as "possessing fever," and that, as you see, is far-fetched.

Ibn Khalawayh reported that Talhah read "fa-immuhu" with a kasrah on the hamzah, and Ibn Duraid related that it is a dialect. As for the grammarians, they say: the hamzah may not be given a kasrah unless it is preceded by a kasrah or a yā'. And Allah knows best.
